(10)), pp. 10-11 (Infinitive tone, ex. (14)). Published chapter pp. 501-532; page numbers not recoverable from the draft.
catalog_quote: The Mara languages have previously been reported as accentual or “two type” languages with fairly reduced or non-existent lexical tonal contrasts (Bastin 2003). However, a closer look at the Mara languages shows that many have more than two lexical tonal contrasts and make use of melodic tones in their verbal systems. [...] The underlying contrast is between H and Ø (toneless) since only H tones are active in the tonal rules. There is at most one lexical H tone per morpheme with the exception of Kabwa double H pattern (see below). Simbiti resembles Kuria in that the TBU is the mora and moras are counted in assigning melodic tones (Marlo, Mwita & Paster 2015). [...] In Simbiti and Ikizu, melodic Hs are shifted from the utterance-final syllable to the penult [...] Simbiti nouns all have a H on the first syllable of the stem, except for a handful of CVVCV-shape nouns that have a H on the noun class prefix in addition to the stem-initial H (10). [...] All six languages lack lexical tonal contrast in the verb stem. In Ikoma (12), Kabwa (13), and Simbiti (14), all verb stems in the Infinitive have a H on the first syllable of the macrostem (the left edge of the macrostem marked with “[”); in Simbiti the H is retracted to the prefix with monosyllabic macrostems.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (29-page Helda author draft of Aunio, Robinson, Roth, Stegen & Walker 2019, 'The Mara languages (JE40)', The Bantu Languages 2nd edn, pp. 501-532; handle 10138/322322 on p. 1) and ran extracted text on pp. 2-3, 7-11. Every sentence of the reported quote is present verbatim at the stated locator: draft p. 7 (section 2.3 'Tone and syllable structure'): 'Simbiti resembles Kuria in that the TBU is the mora and moras are counted in assigning melodic tones (Marlo, Mwita & Paster 2015).' and 'In Simbiti and Ikizu, melodic Hs are shifted from the utterance-final syllable to the penult'; draft p. 9: 'Simbiti nouns all have a H on the first syllable of the stem, except for a handful of CVVCV-s…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Simbiti is described as a tone language (underlying H vs toneless; mora is the tone-bearing unit) and the chapter makes no statement about word stress for Simbiti. Tonal prominence is largely predictable: nouns carry a H on the first stem syllable (a few CVVCV nouns also on the prefix); infinitive verbs carry a H on the first macrostem syllable (on the prefix with monosyllabic stems); other verb forms use four melodic-H patterns assigned by mora counting; a melodic H that would be utterance-final shifts to the penult; a H on one mora of a long vowel spreads to the other mora. Aunio 2015 adds that this syllable-internal doubling gives every word one most prominent syllable (obligatoriness) but longer stems are not culminative. The chapter's remark that the Mara languages 'have previously been reported as accentual' refers to Bastin 2003; regular penultimate stress is reported only for some Zanaki speakers, not Simbiti.
new_statements.exceptions: A handful of CVVCV-shaped nouns carry an additional H on the noun-class prefix (e.g. ɛ̀kɛ́-mɔ́ɔ́ɾì 'calf' vs ɛ̀kɛ̀-tɔ́ɔ́ʃɔ̀ 'hare'); with monosyllabic macrostems the infinitive H is retracted to the prefix (ùkú-[ɲwà 'to drink').
new_statements.domain_note: Word/stem level (noun stem, verb macrostem); tones cited are phrase-medial forms; utterance-final H shifts to the penult. Data from the authors' own fieldwork and SIL Tanzania databases (first-hand).
new_statements.identity_note: Source calls the language 'Simbiti' (= Ethnologue/Glottolog Suba-Simbiti, ISO ssc, Glottolog suba1252; JE431), explicitly distinguished from Kenyan Suba (sxb). Data come from SIL Tanzania's Mara cluster work, presumably the Simbiti variety proper; the ISO request lists dialects Hacha, Kine, Surwa, Sweta, Simbiti and Kiroba. No separate Glottolog dialect codes were used.

M.A. dissertation, Centre for Linguistics, Translation and Literacy, Redcliffe College. 127 pp. (SIL Language & Culture Archives entry 76835, issued 2018-07, status 'preprint').
tone_statements.quote: Simbiti does not have lexical tone. There is grammatical tone on verbs (Walker, 2013), and minimal pairs can occur between the Anterior and Remote Past with vowel-initial verb roots (Walker and Aunio, 2016), for example: 7) βa- andɛk -iɾe → βáːndekíɾe 3PL write PFV ‘they have written’ 8) βa- a- andɛk -iɾe → βaːndekíɾe 3PL PST write PFV ‘they wrote (before today)’ … In this paper, tone is not transcribed unless pertinent to the discussion. … Simbiti is unusual among Mara languages with the tone-bearing unit being the mora (Aunio et al., forthcoming).
tone_statements.locator: p. 22, §2.2.3 Tone and §2.2.4 Moraic Phonology (with fns 16-17)
tone_statements.summary: No lexical tone; grammatical tone on verbs only (underlying high tones on set moras distinguish Anterior from Remote Past); no inventory stated; mora is the tone-bearing unit; tone not.

tone_statements.citation: SIL International, Uganda-Tanzania Branch. 2018. Suba-Simbiti orthography statement (2018 update). Orthography statement, SIL International Uganda-Tanzania Branch; PDF distributed through SIL REAP (sil.org).
tone_statements.quote: There is no lexical tone in Suba‑Simbiti. There is grammatical tone on verbs, and two verb tenses in particular sometimes form tonal minimal pairs. The minimal pairs occur between the Anterior and the Remote Past with certain vowel-initial verb roots. … the Anterior has a high tone underlyingly on the first and fourth moras of the macrostem, and the Remote Past has a high tone underlyingly on the third mora of the macrostem (see Walker and Aunio, 2016, for further details on Simbiti melodic tone pattens).
tone_statements.summary: No lexical tone; grammatical tone on verbs only: Anterior and Remote Past can differ solely by where an underlying high tone falls on the moras of the macrostem. No tone inventory stated.

sources.note: §2.3 Tone and syllable structure: Mara languages 'previously reported as accentual or two-type languages' (Bastin 2003) but have H vs Ø tone; Simbiti has the mora as TBU, nouns all carry H on the stem-initial syllable (a few CVVCV nouns add a prefix H), infinitives carry H on the first macrostem syllable (retracted to the prefix with monosyllabic macrostems), utterance-final melodic Hs shift to the penult, syllable-internal tone spread avoids contours. No word-stress statement for Simbiti; penultimate stress is reported only for (some speakers of) Zanaki and a stress-like system for Nata.

sources.citation: Aunio, Lotta. 2015. A typological perspective on Bantu nominal tone: the case of Ikoma-Nata-Isenye in western Tanzania. Southern African Linguistics and Applied Language Studies 33(3): 359-371. doi:10.2989/16073614.2015.1105106
sources.note: One paragraph on Simbiti (draft p. 12): 'Simbiti (JE431 [ssc]) is underlyingly very different.. since in Simbiti the TBU is the mora.. on the surface there is always one syllable with the highest prominence (obligatoriness) since a tone doubling rule links a H tone associated to only one mora of a long vowel to both moras.. trimoraic and longer nominal stems are not culminative since the H tone can be realised on two syllables.' Tone, not stress.
